html:
The Cahita were a group of peoples in the river valleys of Sinaloa and southern Sonora in northwest Mexico, who spoke related Uto-Aztecan languages. The largest of them were the Yaqui and the Mayo; most of the others have since disappeared.

They farmed maize, beans and squash on the river floodplains and lived in many villages. The Yaqui beat back Spanish expeditions in 1533 and again in the early 1600s, then made peace and invited Jesuit missionaries in 1617. The Jesuits gathered them into eight mission towns, which the Yaqui still treat as their homeland.

The Yaqui fought Mexico again and again in the 1800s, and in the early 1900s many were deported to plantations in Yucatán. The Mayo also survive as a people in Sonora and Sinaloa. See also Cahita on the modern map.
